plain: Many philosophical puzzles come from a misleading picture of how words work. Wittgenstein’s method: look closely at how words are actually used, and the puzzle often loosens.
diagramCaption: Not new facts, but a clearer look at familiar ones.

example.title: “What is time?”
example.text: Asked out of the blue, you are stuck. Yet you use “time” perfectly well every day: “Is it time to go?”, “That took a long time.” Looking at those uses helps more than hunting for a hidden essence of time.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That Wittgenstein offers a set of wise sayings to collect. His later work is closer to a training in looking: the value is in the practice, not the quotations.
insight.matters: Many arguments stall because both sides share a hidden picture. Learning to spot that picture is useful in any field, from law to science to a family disagreement.

askYourself: Which question have I been stuck on because I assumed it must have one hidden answer?
When I say I “don’t understand” something, is information missing, or am I unsure how the words are being used?
What familiar thing would I describe differently if I looked at it slowly?

plain: A sentence can work like a model: its parts stand for things, and how the parts are arranged says how things are. That is why it can be true or false.
diagramCaption: The model shares an arrangement with reality, not a look.

example.title: Explaining a car accident with salt and pepper shakers
example.text: You place the salt for your car and the pepper for the other car. Nobody thinks the shakers are cars, yet the layout shows what happened, and someone could say “No, it was the other way round.”
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That every sentence is literally a little photograph. The point is structural: parts that stand for things, arranged in a way that can match or fail to match.
insight.matters: It separates making sense from being true. You can understand a claim fully before you know whether it is correct, which is exactly what lets you test it.

askYourself: What would have to be the case for this claim I believe to be false?
Which of my maps, charts or plans do I treat as reality rather than as a model of it?
Do I understand this sentence, or do I only know that people say it?

plain: The world is not just a pile of things; it is how those things stand to each other. “The cup is on the book” is a fact. A list of the cup and the book is not.
diagramCaption: Same things, different arrangement, different fact.

example.title: Moving one cup
example.text: A cup, a book and a lamp sit on your desk. Move the cup from the book to the shelf: no new thing appeared, yet what is the case has changed.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That the world is simply the sum of objects in it. In the Tractatus, the world is made of facts: how objects are combined, not a catalogue of them.
insight.matters: Changes often happen in arrangements, not in things. Two situations with the same parts can be entirely different, a useful lens for teams, homes and systems.

askYourself: What in my life changed recently without anything new being added, only rearranged?
When I describe a problem, am I listing things or saying how they stand to each other?
Which arrangement around me would I change first, if I could change only one?

plain: “It is raining” tells you something because it could be false. “It is raining or it is not” is true no matter what, so it tells you nothing about the weather. It shows the structure of logic instead.
diagramCaption: Information rules something out. A logical truth rules nothing out.

example.title: A useless forecast
example.text: A weather app that always says “Rain or no rain tomorrow” is never wrong, and never helpful. Its sentence is perfectly logical and completely empty of news.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That logical truths are pointless because they say nothing. For the Tractatus they are not failed information; they show the structure every informative sentence relies on.
insight.matters: It helps you tell when an argument has given you news and when it has only rearranged what you already assumed.

askYourself: Which of my firm statements could never turn out wrong, and is that a strength or a sign it says nothing?
In the last argument I heard, what new information was actually given?
When I feel certain, is it because of the world or because of how I defined my terms?

plain: Some things cannot be stated in words but can still show themselves, such as the logic of language itself. Wittgenstein says his own book is a ladder: climb it, then put it away.
diagramCaption: Inside: what can be said. The edge itself is only shown.

example.title: Explaining a joke
example.text: You can describe every word of a joke and still not show why it is funny; the humour shows itself when someone gets it. Some understanding is reached rather than stated.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That what cannot be said is unimportant or unreal. The Tractatus suggests almost the opposite: some of what matters most shows itself rather than being stated.
insight.matters: It invites humility about explanation. Some understanding is reached by seeing, practising or living, not by adding one more sentence.

askYourself: What do I know that I have never managed to put into words?
Where have I tried to explain something that someone could only see for themselves?
Which ladder (idea, habit, theory) have I already climbed and could now put down?

plain: “Good” can mean good for a purpose, which you can measure, like a good runner. Ethics is about a different kind of good, and Wittgenstein argues it is not one more fact you could look up.
diagramCaption: A ruler can measure a runner, not the worth of a life.

example.title: Two kinds of “good”
example.text: “That’s a good knife” means it cuts well, and you can test it. “He is a good person” isn’t settled by any test of that kind, though it matters far more.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That Wittgenstein dismisses ethics as meaningless. In the Lecture on Ethics he treats the urge to speak about absolute value with deep respect, while doubting it can be stated as fact.
insight.matters: It keeps two questions apart: “does this work?” and “is this good?” Many decisions blur them.

askYourself: When I call something “good”, do I mean good for a purpose, or good, full stop?
What would I still care about even if every fact were settled?
Which decision this week did I treat as a technical problem when it was really about value?

plain: A language-game is talking and doing woven together. Words get their life from the activities they are part of, like a builder calling “Slab!” and a helper bringing one.
diagramCaption: The word works inside the activity.

example.title: “Scalpel!”
example.text: In surgery, one word is a complete order. Outside the operating room the same word might be a question, a joke or a spelling test. The activity sets its job.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That “language-game” means language is trivial play or that everything is a game. The word stresses activity: speaking is part of doing things together.
insight.matters: Before judging what someone said, ask what they were doing: ordering, joking, warning, reporting. Many misunderstandings are mismatched games.

askYourself: In my last disagreement, were we even playing the same language-game?
Which single word at my work does the job of a whole sentence?
What would someone new to my world need to see, not just hear, to understand our words?

plain: For many words, the meaning is how the word is used, not some object hidden behind it. Words are like tools in a toolbox: they do very different jobs.
diagramCaption: One word, different jobs in different settings.

example.title: “Fine”
example.text: “I’m fine” can mean “I’m well”, “stop asking” or “I’m not fine at all”, depending on tone and situation. You learn what it means by seeing how it is used.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That meaning is “whatever people use a word for”, so anything goes. §43 says use explains meaning for a large class of cases, and use itself has standards.
insight.matters: It frees you from hunting for hidden definitions and turns you toward something you can observe: what a word does here.

askYourself: Which word do I use in two different ways without noticing?
If I stopped asking what a word means and asked what it does, what changes?
What word causes friction between me and someone close to me, and how do we each use it?

plain: Some ideas have no single feature all their cases share. “Game” covers chess, catch and make-believe through overlapping likenesses, like family members who resemble each other in different ways.
diagramCaption: Overlapping fibres make a strong rope.

example.title: What makes something a “sport”?
example.text: Football has teams, golf doesn’t; chess has competition but little running; yoga has skill but no winner. There is no one common feature, yet we use “sport” without trouble.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That family resemblance means concepts are vague or useless. Blurred edges still guide us, the way a rough map still gets you home.
insight.matters: It warns against forcing a single definition where none exists, which matters whenever a label decides how people are treated.

askYourself: Which label do I apply as if it had one essential feature, when it really covers a family?
Where would a strict definition do more harm than a set of good examples?
What are three very different things I call by the same name, and what links each pair?

plain: Language rests on shared ways of living: how we greet, count, trade, play and grieve. Understanding words means sharing enough of the life they belong to.
diagramCaption: Words grow out of what we do together.

example.title: Tipping abroad
example.text: A traveller can know the word for “tip” and still be lost about when to give one, how much, and what it means. The word only makes sense against a whole practice.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That “form of life” means each culture lives in a sealed bubble and cannot be judged or understood from outside. The term points to shared human background, not a license for relativism.
insight.matters: Understanding someone may require sharing more than vocabulary: their practices, timing, gestures and stakes.

askYourself: Which of my habits would make my words hard to understand for someone outside my life?
What practice gives my most important words their sense?
When I misunderstood someone recently, was it the words or the life around them?

plain: Knowing a rule means being able to go on correctly in new cases. No formula or inner flash forces the next step; training and shared practice do.
diagramCaption: After 1000, “add 2” needs a practice behind it.

example.title: Learning to knit
example.text: The pattern says “knit two, purl two”. You understand it when your hands can keep going row after row, not when you can recite it.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That rule-following is a mystery with no answer, so “anything could be correct”. The remarks show correctness lives in shared practice, training and correction.
insight.matters: It changes how you think about learning: understanding shows in what you can do next, not in a feeling of having got it.

askYourself: What do I “understand” in theory but can’t yet go on with in practice?
Who taught me how to continue a practice I now take for granted?
When someone surprises me by following a rule differently, what did our training leave open?

plain: If every rule needed another rule to explain how to apply it, we would never act. At some point we simply follow it; understanding shows in what we do.
diagramCaption: An endless chain of interpretations never reaches an action.

example.title: Instructions that never end
example.text: Imagine a recipe that says “season to taste”, then a note explaining “to taste”, then a note explaining that note… A cook just tastes and adds salt.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That because any rule can be interpreted many ways, there is no right way to follow it. Wittgenstein’s point is that grasping a rule is not an interpretation at all.
insight.matters: It explains why endless clarification can make things worse. At some point action, not another explanation, shows understanding.

askYourself: Where am I asking for one more explanation instead of trying?
Which instructions do I follow perfectly without being able to justify them?
When did a discussion of “what we really meant” stop helping?

plain: Could someone invent a word that only they could ever understand, for a sensation only they could check? Wittgenstein argues such a sign would have no standard of correct use.
diagramCaption: A public word can be corrected. A purely private sign can’t.

example.title: The diary of “S”
example.text: Someone writes “S” in a diary whenever a certain feeling comes back. But what decides whether today’s feeling is really the same one? If only memory decides, “seems right” and “is right” can’t come apart.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That Wittgenstein denies private feelings or inner life. The target is a language whose meaning could be fixed only by one person’s inner impressions.
insight.matters: It shows how deeply public our words for feelings are, which can make us both more careful and more confident when we speak about what we feel.

askYourself: How did I learn the word for the feeling I find hardest to describe?
When I say “no one could understand how I feel”, what exactly is out of reach?
How do I check whether I am using a feeling word the same way as before?

plain: Imagine everyone has a box with a “beetle” that no one else can see. The word “beetle” still works, so what is in the box plays no part in the word’s shared meaning.
diagramCaption: No one sees into another box, and the word still works.

example.title: “Tastes like coriander”
example.text: You can’t compare your taste experience with mine directly, yet we both say coriander is soapy or fresh and argue about it. The shared word lives in what we say and do.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That the beetle example says experiences don’t exist. It says the private object drops out of the word’s public meaning, not out of life.
insight.matters: We can talk meaningfully about feelings without comparing hidden contents, which can ease worries about whether anyone ever truly understands us.

askYourself: Which of my words would still work even if what “is in my box” were different?
Where do I assume others feel exactly as I do because we use the same word?
What would it mean to understand someone’s pain without having it?

plain: A criterion is what counts as something; evidence only makes it likely. Rain falling counts as rain; wet streets are evidence of rain.
diagramCaption: What counts as rain versus what suggests rain.

example.title: Is the cake done?
example.text: A clean toothpick is evidence that the cake is baked. Being cooked through is what being done means. Evidence can mislead; that is why we still sometimes cut into a raw cake.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That criteria are infallible proofs. Wittgenstein’s view is debated, but criteria concern what counts as something, and circumstances can still defeat a judgement.
insight.matters: Separating “what counts as X” from “what suggests X” sharpens decisions in medicine, hiring, grading and everyday trust.

askYourself: What am I treating as proof that is only evidence?
What, for me, counts as someone being kind, honest or rested?
Which of my judgements would change if I changed my criteria rather than gathering more evidence?

plain: You can look at the same picture and suddenly see it differently, like a cube that flips. Nothing on the paper changed, yet what you see did.
diagramCaption: Same lines, two ways of seeing.

example.title: A familiar face in a stranger
example.text: You look at a stranger and suddenly see your brother’s smile in them. Their face hasn’t changed, but now you can’t unsee the likeness.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That seeing an aspect is just adding an interpretation in words. The change is in the seeing itself, though it depends on concepts and abilities.
insight.matters: Insight often means seeing the same material differently. Nothing new arrives, yet everything looks changed.

askYourself: What in my life have I suddenly seen differently, though nothing about it changed?
Which aspect of a person close to me have I stopped being able to see?
What would help someone see the aspect I see, without forcing them?

plain: Some certainties are not conclusions we reached but the hinges our questions turn on, like “I have hands” or “the earth existed long before me”. Doubt needs something that stays fixed.
diagramCaption: The door moves only because the hinges stay put.

example.title: Checking a bank statement
example.text: You can doubt one charge and check it, but only because you take for granted that the numbers on the page don’t change while you read them.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That hinge certainties are proven truths or arbitrary dogmas. They function as the background that makes checking possible, and that role can shift over time.
insight.matters: Knowing which beliefs are hinges for you helps you argue honestly: some disagreements are about evidence, others about what stands fast.

askYourself: What do I never check because checking anything depends on it?
Which of my hinges has moved over the years?
In a deep disagreement, are we arguing about evidence or about what stands fast?

plain: A real doubt needs a reason and a way to check. “Did I lock the door?” is a working doubt; “Do I have hands?” has no test that could settle it, so it isn’t really doubting.
diagramCaption: Doubt that can be checked versus doubt with nowhere to go.

example.title: The locked door
example.text: Halfway to work, you wonder if you locked the door. You can go back, try the handle and settle it. Doubting whether the door exists at all would leave you nothing to check.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That Wittgenstein refutes skepticism with a knock-down proof. He asks what doubting needs in order to be real doubt, which changes the question rather than ending it.
insight.matters: It helps you match checking to stakes: doubt where a mistake is possible and testable, and notice when anxiety imitates doubt.

askYourself: Which of my worries has a way to check, and which has none?
What would count as settling my current doubt?
Where am I checking far more, or far less, than the situation warrants?

plain: Some colour questions are for science (why does this look lighter?) and some are about our concepts (could there be a see-through white?). Wittgenstein separates the two.
diagramCaption: One puzzle, two kinds of question.

example.title: Transparent white
example.text: Green glass makes things look green. But a “white glass” would just look milky; things behind it wouldn’t look white. The puzzle is about how “white” works, not about physics.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That the colour remarks are amateur optics. They investigate the logic of colour words, which no experiment alone can settle.
insight.matters: Learning to separate a factual question from a conceptual one saves time and confusion, in science and in arguments.

askYourself: Is the question I’m stuck on answered by finding out, or by clarifying what I mean?
Which word do I use precisely in one setting and loosely in another?
What colour (or taste, or sound) can I not put into words at all?

plain: Being predictable is not the same as being forced. A law of nature describes what tends to happen; it doesn’t push you to act.
diagramCaption: A regularity is not a hand on your back.

example.title: Your morning coffee
example.text: Your friend can predict you’ll order coffee at 8 a.m. That prediction doesn’t make you order it; you do, for your own reasons.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That because behaviour can be predicted, it must be forced. The lecture separates regularity, prediction and compulsion, though the debate stays open.
insight.matters: It frees ordinary talk of choosing from a picture of invisible hands pushing us, while staying honest about patterns.

askYourself: Which of my habits do I describe as if I were forced?
When someone predicts my choice, does that make it less mine?
What do I mean when I say I “had no choice”?

plain: In Wittgenstein’s sense, a word’s grammar is the rules for using it, much like a chess king is defined by how it may move, not by its shape.
diagramCaption: The rules for moving it make it a king.

example.title: A bottle cap as a king
example.text: Lose the king from a chess set and use a bottle cap instead. It works perfectly, because what makes it the king is the moves allowed, not the carving.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That Wittgenstein’s grammar is school grammar. It is the network of rules for using a word: what follows from it, what makes sense to say with it.
insight.matters: Many “deep” puzzles turn out to be grammatical: they come from using a word outside the setting that gives it sense.

askYourself: What can and can’t sensibly be said with a word I care about, like “love” or “success”?
Which question of mine sounds deep but mixes the grammar of two different words?
What would a beginner need to learn to use one of my professional terms correctly?

plain: Rituals are not always bad attempts at science. Kissing a photo of someone you love isn’t a mistaken prediction that the kiss will reach them; it expresses love.
diagramCaption: An act can express something without trying to cause something.

example.title: Blowing out birthday candles
example.text: No one thinks the candles physically grant wishes, yet the act is full of meaning. Asking “does it work?” misses what it means.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That Wittgenstein simply defends rituals as beyond criticism. He questions one interpreter’s assumption that all ritual is failed science; criticism remains possible.
insight.matters: It invites respect before judgement: ask what an act expresses in a life before asking whether it works.

askYourself: Which of my own rituals would look irrational to an outsider, and what do they express?
Where have I judged someone’s practice as a mistake when it was an expression?
What would be lost if I explained one of my rituals away?

plain: We learn words for feelings through how feelings show (wincing, saying “ouch”) in situations like a burn or a fall. The critic Peacocke asks whether this explains everything about experience.
diagramCaption: Experience, expression and circumstances, learned together.

example.title: Learning “ouch”
example.text: A toddler bumps a knee, cries, and a parent says “Ouch! That hurts.” The child learns “hurt” from the bump, the crying and the comfort together, not by pointing inward.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That feelings are “just behaviour”. The remarks connect experience with expression and circumstances without reducing one to the other, and critics like Peacocke press on the gaps.
insight.matters: It makes room for both your inner life and the public ways we come to understand it.

askYourself: How do I usually show a feeling I rarely name?
What circumstances make my feelings easy or hard for others to read?
Is there an experience of mine that no expression seems to capture?

plain: Philosophy, for Wittgenstein, is not about discovering new facts but about clearing up confusion by arranging what we already know, so we can see our way out.
diagramCaption: A fly in a bottle: the way out was always open.

example.title: Lost in your own home
example.text: In a dark room you bump into furniture you know well. Turning on the light adds nothing new to the room; it lets you see what was already there.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That philosophy, for Wittgenstein, is pointless or merely negative. Clarification is the work: arranging what we know so a confusion dissolves.
insight.matters: Not every problem needs more data. Some need a better arrangement of what is already in front of us.

askYourself: Which problem of mine needs a clearer view rather than more information?
What is my fly-bottle: the familiar picture I keep bumping against?
What reminder would help me most this week?

plain: Read a numbered remark slowly: find exactly which edition and section it is, notice who is speaking, what idea it targets, which hedges matter, and what you think.
diagramCaption: Five steps for reading a remark closely.

example.title: Reading §43
example.text: Note the hedge: meaning is use “for a large class of cases”, not for all. Dropping those words turns a careful remark into a slogan.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That a famous line can be quoted on its own. Remarks are often dialogues with qualifications; lifting them out can reverse their sense.
insight.matters: Close reading is a transferable skill: it protects you from slogans in any field.

askYourself: Which quotation do I repeat without knowing its context?
Whose voice is speaking in the sentence I just read: the author’s, or an objector’s?
What qualification in a text did I skip because it was inconvenient?

plain: Bring the tools into an ordinary day: notice a word doing too much work, look at how it is used here, compare cases, decide, and stay open to correction.
diagramCaption: A small, repeatable habit.

example.title: “Productive”
example.text: Your team argues about whether a week was “productive”. Ask: productive in which sense? Shipped work, learning, rest? The argument often turns out to be several smaller, answerable questions.
example.label: Invented example

insight.misreading: That Wittgenstein provides a complete method for living well. He offers tools for clearer seeing, which leave room for evidence, ethics and other people.
insight.matters: Small habits of attention to words make disagreements more precise and kinder.

askYourself: Which word did too much work in my day today?
What question would make tomorrow’s hardest conversation more precise?
Which of today’s certainties should stay open to correction?
